domains.name: Type of technology
domains.intro: Start with the kind of technology you are evaluating. What it is shapes which questions matter as you go.

questions.text: What kind of technology are you evaluating?

options.label: mHealth app
options.note: A phone app that supports health or well-being — mood tracking, meditation, symptom journals, and similar. It may collect personal information as it works.

options.label: Chatbot
options.note: A program that talks with you in text. It can feel like a conversation, but there may be no real person behind it.

options.label: Social media
options.note: A platform where people post and share content. It is built to hold attention, and what people share there is often public.

options.label: Forum or group chat
options.note: A space where a group of people talk together online, usually around a shared topic or experience.

options.label: Something else
options.note: A game, a wearable, a website, or something different. The questions ahead still apply — note anything specific as you go.

domains.name: Quality of technology
domains.intro: Look at what stands behind the technology: who made it, what supports it, and how it treats the people who use it.

questions.text: Is it clear who made this technology, and why?

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Spend a few minutes looking into who is behind it — an about page, the company name, a news search — before going further.

options.label: No
options.note: Treat its claims with extra caution. When it is unclear who is behind a product, there is no one to hold accountable if something goes wrong.

questions.text: Is there evidence that it works?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Look at what the evidence covers, and who it was tested with. Results for one group do not always carry over to others.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Look for research, a public evaluation, or a study behind the claims. If you cannot find one, treat it as unproven for now.

options.label: No
options.note: If nothing backs up its claims, its promises may not hold up in practice. Weigh that before trusting it with someone's mental health.

questions.text: If someone needs urgent help while using it, does the technology show them where to get it?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Check that the path to help is easy to find — reachable from the main screens, not buried in a corner.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Open it and picture a hard moment: where would someone go? If you cannot find a path, assume there is not one.

options.label: No
options.note: People may turn to it when they are struggling. Without a clear path to real help, it should not be anyone's only source of support.

questions.text: Does it explain, in plain language, what happens to what you share?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Check the explanation against what the app actually asks for. See whether it can be used without sharing more than you want to.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Look for a privacy notice you can read and understand. If it is missing or hard to find, that is worth weighing on its own.

options.label: No
options.note: If it does not say what happens to your information, assume it collects and shares more than you would expect.

questions.text: Does it use design features meant to keep people coming back?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Streaks, constant reminders, and rewards for returning are built to hold attention. Ask whether that pull fits the person using it — and how it would feel to set it down.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Watch for the usual signals: notifications, streak counters, rewards for checking in. If you spot any of them, weigh it as a yes for now.

questions.text: For a chatbot: when it cannot help, does a real person take over?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Proceed with caution: a human safeguard is a good sign, but keep working through the other questions.

options.label: No
options.note: If you cannot tell whether a person takes over, treat it as a no for now. Without a person in the loop, a chatbot cannot catch it when things go wrong — consider an MHCC-certified chatbot instead.

domains.guidance: Look at the pattern across your answers, not any single one. A technology with clear accountability, real evidence, and a safety net is easier to trust. Where the picture is mixed, decide which gaps matter most in your situation — and what would need to change before you would rely on it.

domains.name: User considerations
domains.intro: Now the person who will use it. Quality is not the whole story — fit, support, and watchfulness matter just as much.

questions.text: Does the person using it know what could go wrong?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Good — knowing the risks is what lets someone notice them early.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Walk it through together: what it does with information, what it cannot do, and what it is not a replacement for.

options.label: No
options.note: Go through the basics before it gets used. Someone who does not know the risks cannot watch for them.

questions.text: If something goes wrong, does the person know where to turn?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Good — knowing the way back is part of using anything safely.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Work it out together before it is needed: who to tell if something feels off, and how to reach them.

options.label: No
options.note: Make a small plan now: one person to tell, and one way to reach them. That is the difference between a problem and a dead end.

questions.text: Does the person's age or situation call for extra care right now?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Match the support to it: check in more often, and sooner. Age and hard seasons both change what a technology should be asked to carry.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: When in doubt, lean toward more support. It is easier to step back later than to catch up after a problem.

questions.text: Will an adult be nearby or checking in?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Good. Agree on what checking in looks like — regular enough to matter, light enough that it does not push the person to hide their use.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Settle this before it matters: who checks in, and how often.

options.label: No
options.note: Ask whether that changes the choice. For a younger or more vulnerable person, a nearby adult is often what turns a tool into a support.

questions.text: How much of the person's day does it take up?

options.label: A fair amount
options.note: Worth watching. Check that it is not quietly crowding out other things.

options.label: A lot
options.note: A lot of time with any technology pushes other things out — sleep, people, getting outside. Look at what it is displacing.

options.label: Not sure
options.note: Keep an eye on it for a week. Amounts are easier to see in hindsight than in the moment.

domains.guidance: Fit matters as much as quality. The same technology can be a good choice for one person and a poor one for another, depending on age, situation, and the support around them. Where something gives you pause, trust the pause — raise the support, or step back, and talk it over with someone you trust.
